title: How banknotes are made hard to fake

explain.say: A banknote is just printed paper or plastic, so why can't anyone print their own at home? Because notes hide secret features! Experts teach a checklist: feel, look, tilt. Look at step one: feel. Real notes feel crisp, and some printing is raised, so you can feel it with a fingertip.

explain.say: See the wire? Most notes have a security thread running through them. On Indian rupee notes, the thread shows the words Bharat and RBI, and it changes colour from green to blue when you tilt it. Can you find the thread on a note at home?

faq.q: Why does a real banknote feel different?
faq.a: Notes are made from special cotton paper or polymer plastic, not normal paper, and some parts are printed with raised ink you can feel.
A faint picture inside the paper, made by changing the paper's thickness while it is made. You see it when you hold the note up to the light.
asks: How do I see the watermark?

faq.a: Holograms and colour-changing inks look different from every angle, which ordinary printers and copiers can't copy.
asks: What is the shiny strip on money?

faq.q: What should you do if you think a note is fake?
faq.a: Don't try to spend it. Give it to a grown-up, who can take it to a bank or the police; knowingly passing on a fake note is a crime.
asks: What if I get a fake note?

faq.q: Which country made the first plastic banknotes?
faq.a: Australia, in 1988. Polymer notes last longer than paper ones and can have see-through windows that are hard to fake.

facts: Australia issued the world's first polymer banknotes in 1988.
Watermarks are made by varying the thickness of the paper as it is formed.
